content: Each year, influenza virus infections result in significant illness and death in the United States. The primary method of preventing influenza is through vaccination. Historically, only the inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV), administered via injection, was available in the U.S. This vaccine is approved for individuals aged six months and older, including those with chronic medical conditions. In 2003, a new intranasal, trivalent, cold-adapted, live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) was approved for use in healthy individuals aged 5–49 years. LAIV provides an alternative for vaccinating healthy individuals in this age group who wish to avoid influenza or who are in close contact with individuals at high risk for severe influenza complications. LAIVs have been used in Russia and have been under development in the U.S. since the 1960s. They have been evaluated in monovalent, bivalent, and trivalent formulations. The U.S.-approved LAIV, marketed as FluMist™, is a live, trivalent vaccine administered intranasally. It is attenuated, meaning it causes mild or no symptoms related to influenza infection. It is temperature-sensitive, limiting replication of the vaccine virus at 38–39°C, thereby restricting its replication in the lower respiratory tract. It is also cold-adapted, replicating efficiently at 25°C, a temperature that supports LAIV virus replication but restricts wild-type virus replication. In animal studies, LAIV viruses replicate in the nasopharyngeal mucosa, inducing protective immunity. The development of LAIV involved creating two stably attenuated master donor viruses (MDVs), one for influenza A and one for influenza B. These MDVs acquired their cold-adapted, temperature-sensitive, and attenuated phenotypes through serial passage in viral cultures at progressively lower temperatures. The vaccine viruses in LAIV are reassortant viruses containing genes from these MDVs, which confer attenuation, temperature sensitivity, and cold adaptation, as well as genes from contemporary wild-type influenza viruses encoding the surface antigens hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). The MDVs serve as the attenuated vehicles for presenting influenza HA and NA antigens to the immune system, eliciting a protective antibody response. The reassortant vaccine viruses are grown in embryonated hen’s eggs. After formulation, the vaccine is stored at -15°C or colder and administered intranasally. The immunogenicity of LAIV has been evaluated in multiple studies involving approximately 100 children aged 5–17 years and 300 adults aged 18–49 years. LAIV viruses primarily replicate in nasopharyngeal epithelial cells. The protective mechanisms induced by LAIV vaccination are not fully understood but likely involve both serum and nasal secretory antibodies. No single laboratory measurement closely correlates with the protective immunity induced by LAIV. Both LAIV and IIV contain influenza virus strains antigenically equivalent to the annually recommended strains: one influenza A (H3N2) virus, one A (H1N1) virus, and one B virus. Virus strains may change annually based on global surveillance and the emergence of new strains. Both vaccines are grown in eggs and are administered annually to provide optimal protection against influenza infection. Key differences between LAIV and IIV include their composition and administration routes. IIV contains killed viruses, while LAIV contains live attenuated viruses capable of replication. LAIV is administered intranasally via a sprayer, whereas IIV is administered intramuscularly via injection. LAIV is more expensive than IIV and is approved only for healthy individuals aged 5–49 years, while IIV is approved for individuals aged six months and older, including those with chronic medical conditions. The efficacy of LAIV has been demonstrated in randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials. Among healthy children aged 15–71 months, LAIV showed 93% efficacy during a season with well-matched vaccine and circulating virus strains. In a subsequent season with a less well-matched A (H3N2) component, efficacy was 86%. LAIV also reduced febrile otitis media and antibiotic use. Among healthy adults aged 18–64 years, LAIV reduced severe febrile illnesses, febrile upper respiratory tract illnesses, days of illness, work absenteeism, and healthcare visits. In a challenge study, LAIV demonstrated 85% efficacy in preventing laboratory-confirmed influenza, compared to 71% for IIV, though the difference was not statistically significant. Because LAIV contains live influenza viruses, there is potential for transmission of vaccine viruses to others. However, studies have shown that vaccine viruses shed by recipients are phenotypically stable and retain their attenuated, cold-adapted, and temperature-sensitive properties. Transmission of vaccine viruses to close contacts is rare and has not been associated with significant illness. Recommendations for influenza vaccination prioritize specific groups, including individuals at high risk for complications due to age or medical conditions, and those in close contact with high-risk individuals. LAIV is an option for healthy individuals aged 5–49 years, including those in close contact with high-risk groups. However, LAIV is not recommended for certain populations, such as immunocompromised individuals, children under five years, or adults over 50 years. LAIV must be stored at -15°C or colder and should not be stored in frost-free freezers due to potential temperature fluctuations. It must be thawed before administration and should not be refrozen. The vaccine is administered intranasally, with half the dose sprayed into each nostril. If the recipient sneezes after administration, the dose should not be repeated. Side effects of LAIV are generally mild and self-limited. Among children, common side effects include runny nose, headache, fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, and muscle aches. Among adults, runny nose, headache, and sore throat are more common. LAIV is not approved for use in children under 60 months due to an observed increase in asthma or reactive airway disease in this age group. In summary, LAIV offers an effective and convenient alternative to IIV for healthy individuals aged 5–49 years. Its intranasal administration and ability to induce mucosal immunity make it a valuable option for influenza prevention. However, its use is limited to specific populations, and careful consideration of contraindications and storage requirements is essential.
